c.tagline: Legendary Saharan caravan city of mud-brick mosques and ancient manuscripts.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps; getting around means shared bush taxis, hired 4x4s or arranged drivers, with fares agreed in cash beforehand.

emergency.note: 17 reaches the police and 15 the ambulance service; emergency coverage is very limited outside major towns.

avoid.reason: Foreign governments advise against all travel to Timbuktu and northern Mali due to terrorism and kidnapping — the entire area is effectively off-limits to tourists.
Kidnap and banditry risk extends to every overland and river route into the city; any travel requires professional security arrangements.

hood_desc: The oldest and most central quarter, built around Mansa Musa's 1327 Djinguereber Mosque — the great mud-brick landmark of the city; the usual base, close to the market and most guesthouses.
The scholarly quarter to the north around the Sankoré Mosque, once the heart of Timbuktu's medieval university and manuscript libraries; a dense grid of earthen houses and Quranic schools.
A traditional residential quarter of low mud-brick homes and small courtyards away from the main monuments; quiet, local, and everyday rather than touristed.
The newer district on the edge of town toward the airport and administrative offices, with wider sandy streets and larger compounds; where much of modern civic life sits.

water.note: Drink only bottled or properly treated water.

transit.hours: Shared taxis and motorbikes run mostly in daylight; there is no scheduled service.
transit.note: Timbuktu has no formal public transport; people walk or use shared taxis, motorbikes and donkey carts, while the Niger River port of Kabara (~18 km south) links the city to river pinasses.
transit.pay: All fares are paid in cash (CFA francs), negotiated with the driver or boatman in advance.

sys.n: Niger River pinasse via Kabara port

bus: Long-distance buses & 4x4 bush taxis to Mopti, Sévaré and Bamako (rough desert-edge roads)
ferry: Niger River pinasses from Kabara port to Mopti/Gao (seasonal, water-level dependent)

transit.m: Shared taxi or arranged 4x4 to the town centre (~10 min)

tip.r: Tipping isn't formalised; a small cash tip for guides, drivers and hotel staff is appreciated.

food.name: Takula (Mud-Oven Flatbread)
food.desc: Timbuktu's own bread: flat rounds of wheat dough baked in beehive-shaped mud ovens, eaten torn into sauce or split around grilled meat.

places.name: Sankore mud-oven bakeries
places.note: Highest concentration of beehive ovens in the city, north of the Monument des Martyrs; buy it hot at dawn.

places.name: Grand Marche
places.note: Bread sellers bring takula in from the neighbourhood ovens each morning to the central market.

places.name: Restaurant Le Souvenir
places.note: Serves takula with local sauces as part of its Malian menu rather than imported baguette.

food.name: Rice with Sauce
food.desc: The Malian daily plate: rice under a groundnut, tomato or okra sauce with a piece of mutton or fish. Riz au gras is the richer, one-pot version.

places.name: Restaurant Le Souvenir
places.note: Straightforward Malian cooking; the rice-and-sauce plate is the thing to order.

places.name: Poulet d'Or
places.note: Small restaurant doing rice, sauce and grilled chicken; one of the few consistent sit-down options.

places.name: Grand Marche food stalls
places.note: Market cooks ladle rice and sauce into bowls from midday; cheapest meal in Timbuktu.

food.name: Grilled Capitaine from the Niger
food.desc: Nile perch brought up from the river port at Kabara, split, salted and grilled over charcoal. The freshest protein in a city on the desert's edge.

places.name: Restaurant Le Coucher du Soleil
places.note: Serves Malian dishes with a sunset view over the dunes; grilled fish when the river boats deliver.

places.name: Grand Marche grill stalls
places.note: Charcoal grills beside the market cook fish and mutton to order in the late afternoon.

places.name: Kabara road fish sellers
places.note: The river port supplying Timbuktu; fish arrives here first and is grilled at roadside stands.

food.name: Mechoui (Grilled Mutton)
food.desc: Whole or jointed sheep rubbed with salt and spice and roasted slowly over coals or in a sand pit, then torn apart by hand. The Saharan feast dish.

places.name: Grand Marche grill stalls
places.note: Butchers grill mutton over charcoal through the afternoon; sold by weight with bread and onion.

places.name: Restaurant Le Coucher du Soleil
places.note: Arranges whole-lamb grills for groups at the dune camps outside the city.

places.name: Tuareg camps on the north dunes
places.note: Desert camps roast mutton for visiting groups as part of an overnight in the dunes.

food.name: Timbuktu Dates
food.desc: Dates from the palm gardens fringing the city, sold loose by the scoop. A staple of caravan travel and still the everyday sweet with tea.

places.name: Grand Marche
places.note: Date sellers work the same stalls as the salt slab traders; taste before you buy.

places.name: Sankore quarter shops
places.note: Small provision shops near the mosque sell dates, peanuts and dried fruit by weight.

places.name: Cafe Ali
places.note: Serves dates and dried fruit with coffee and juice; easy place to try them sitting down.

food.name: Millet To with Sauce
food.desc: Stiff millet or sorghum porridge stirred over a fire and dipped into okra, baobab-leaf or groundnut sauce. The oldest everyday food of the Sahel.

places.name: Grand Marche food stalls
places.note: Women sell to and sauce from big pots at lunchtime; the true local staple rather than a tourist dish.

places.name: Restaurant Le Souvenir
places.note: Cooks to alongside rice for visitors wanting the traditional Sahelian version.

places.name: Sankore neighbourhood kitchens
places.note: Home kitchens and small stands in the old quarter serve to in the evening.

food.name: Tuareg Green Tea
food.desc: Gunpowder green tea brewed over charcoal and poured from height in three rounds: bitter as life, sweet as love, mild as death. The ritual takes an hour.

places.name: Cafe Ali
places.note: Central cafe where tea is brewed properly over coals; also does coffee and fruit juices.

places.name: Tuareg camps on the north dunes
places.note: The full three-round ceremony as it is meant to be done, sitting on mats after dark.

places.name: Grand Marche tea stands
places.note: Traders brew tea between customers all day; joining a round is an ordinary courtesy here.

food.name: Dableni (Hibiscus Juice)
food.desc: Dried hibiscus calyxes boiled with sugar and ginger and served ice cold. Deep red, tart and the standard cooling drink across Mali.

places.name: Cafe Ali
places.note: Fresh juices and smoothies including hibiscus and baobab, served cold, a rarity in the heat.

places.name: Grand Marche juice sellers
places.note: Hibiscus and ginger juice sold in frozen sachets and bottles at the market for very little.

places.name: Restaurant Le Souvenir
places.note: Serves local juices with meals; Timbuktu is dry, so these are what accompany dinner.

landmarks: Djinguereber Mosque
The city's great Friday mosque, raised in 1327 for Emperor Mansa Musa, is a UNESCO-listed masterpiece of earthen architecture bristling with wooden support beams.
Sankore Mosque and University
Once the intellectual heart of a university teaching 25,000 students, this pyramid-minareted mud mosque symbolises Timbuktu's golden age of Islamic scholarship.
Sidi Yahya Mosque
The third of Timbuktu's great mosques, founded around 1440, guards ornate doors long said to remain closed until the end of the world.
Ahmed Baba Institute of Higher Learning
A modern sanctuary for tens of thousands of medieval Arabic manuscripts, preserving the astronomical, legal and poetic brilliance of Timbuktu's scholarly heritage.
Heinrich Barth House
The mud-brick dwelling where the German explorer lodged in 1853-54, now a small museum honouring the scholarly traveller who documented Timbuktu for Europe.
René Caillié House
A plaque marks the humble house sheltering the first European to reach Timbuktu and return alive, the Frenchman who won Paris's prize in 1828.
Gordon Laing House
The residence of the ill-fated Scottish major, first European to arrive in 1826 before being murdered in the desert, stands as a haunting explorer's landmark.
Well of Old Bouctou
The legendary well tended by the woman Bouctou, from whom the city takes its name, marks the caravan camp that grew into a Saharan metropolis.
Flame of Peace Monument
A monument of encased weapons commemorates the 1996 ceremony when 3,000 guns were burned to seal peace between Mali's government and Tuareg rebels.
Grand Marché and Saharan Dunes
Timbuktu's covered market trades salt slabs and desert crafts, while camel treks from town reach Tuareg camps amid the rolling Saharan sands.

bus.note: Overland links run by 4x4 bush taxi and rough bus to Mopti/Sévaré (~200 km) and on to Bamako; routes are long, unpaved in places and security-dependent.

intl.to: Mopti & Gao (Mali) - seasonal Niger River pinasses from Kabara, ~18 km south, mainly Aug-Dec
intl.op: local operators — arranged at the river port

ferry.note: Seasonal Niger River pinasses (large motorised pirogues) connect the river port of Kabara, ~18 km south, with Mopti and Gao when water levels allow, mainly August-December.

half.name: Lac Faguibine
half.blurb: Lac Faguibine is a large seasonal lake northwest of Timbuktu that fills with the Niger River's annual flood pulse.

full.name: Niafunke
full.blurb: Niafunke is a Niger River town south of Timbuktu known as the home of Grammy-winning musician Ali Farka Toure.
